chapter: Early listening, piano and adolescent conflict
title: Ben Webster, the struggle of artists and Ellington's band
summary: Asked about Ben Webster, Thompson describes his struggles, his rank among tenors with Hawkins, Young and Chu Berry, and how he and Blanton revived Duke Ellington's band.

story.theme_name: Duke Ellington and his orchestra, as others knew them
story.community_name: Duke Ellington: the band, the man, his men

blocks.x: Well, what I want to know too is your approach to your talents. I mean, some people are burdened with their talents, there are people that are -- there are people that have to fight their talents. You know, I'm thinking of Ben Webster, for instance. Another -- I mean, he was tremendously talented and yet he had to fight that horn and fight himself and what not. And usually people that feel deeply too, you know.
But did you slave away at your talent or were you able to take it in your stride and develop it as you went along

Well, I think my approach to music is like most people, in fact you mentioned Ben Webster. And I happen to know quite a bit about Ben Webster as a person and as a human being and as a fellow who as I said my father gave me some instructions in psychology and what not at an early age. That makes it easy for me to detect certain peculiarities in people. And I think that Ben Webster probably had the same struggle that all musicians have, but it affected him differently and how he carried his self in personal life, and his habits and so forth, had to do with his atrocities --

Or his confusion that you speak of. And I felt very close to Ben Webster. I believe he was born on the same astrological sign as I, Aries. And I admired his work, and the fact of the matter is if you want to speak in terms of competition, there was quite some controversy for the many early years of jazz that Ben Webster perhaps was classed as one of the top three or four tenor saxophone players in those days when there was Coleman Hawkins considered to be the father, the grandfather, and the originator of the true musical approach to the jazz saxophone, opposed to Lester Young's more loose expressions of down to earth playing and sounds of rhythmic meter.
And then there was Chu Berry who also had a different

musical approach. And Ben Webster had his own qualities, which was classified along with these great tenor saxophone players, you know. But as I said, I think that his struggle, and it's the same -- I think every artist in any field has this and I think they have to deal with this. And it comes apart in your life, and I've had my share of it and I'm having my share of it now. And you asked me did I struggle. Yes, I'm still struggling because it starts with your ability to improve yourself. And this comes in technical part of music like I'll never forget when I went to the army, one of the young guys caught me off guard, and he said you're a musician. I said, yes, I've been making a living playing music all my life. He said, how many sharps are there in F sharp, you know. You know, he caught me off guard. Right this minute I'm not too sure I can tell you.

I mean things of that sort are a challenge to you, no matter how great you are. And Ben Webster certainly was one of the most influential parts of Duke Ellington's band in the forties. Up to that point Duke's band had been featuring the saxophone more or less of Johnny Hodges. But Ben Webster actually gave Duke a new life, along with a bass player by the name of Jimmy Blanton. Between the two of these guys they brought new life to Duke Ellington's band, which made it able for him to compete musically with the other bands who were beginning to become popular, such as Count Basie and of
course Earl Hines who had always had a very fine rhythmic orchestration of musicians, you see.

So actually this struggle, I have had that struggle and I still have that struggle. This is part of being an artist, and particularly one who's making a living at the field. And in that sense I could say yes, I've had struggles and I'm still having struggles with myself, in trying to play.
